key_facts: Indian workers in Bengaluru, including barber Mohammed Ashim, wear head-mounted cameras for 5-6 hours a day to record their hands and fingers while performing tasks; client faces are blurred, and the footage is sold to technology companies and research organisations for training so-called physical AI (robot-controlling AI).

Rashdan Technologies pays $5 to $10 (£3.74; £7.47) for eight to 10 hours of recorded work; clients are now requesting four to six cameras around a person's head, and such higher-tier collection is paid more. Humyn Labs has 96,000 data collectors across Latin America and Southeast Asia.

Humyn Labs founder Manish Agarwal argues that physical tasks require high-quality signals involving limb movements and force application, and that no existing internet archive of embodied human activity exists, so the data must be captured from scratch.
Bino Paul, senior professor at TISS, says it is too early to tell whether this work will lead to robots automating workers' jobs, and calls for government regulation of AI.
importance_reason: Feature-style piece on labour and AI data collection without direct market-moving event; limited near-term economic impact.
